vignette:
The Weight of What He Carries

Marco is a 37-year-old Colombian-born man who has spent the better part of a decade working for a community outreach organization, connecting vulnerable families in his city to food assistance, housing resources, and crisis support. He is the person others call when they don't know where else to turn. He is good at this — patient, warm, and fluent in the particular language of suffering. What almost no one in his life knows is that he has his own story he has never fully told.

For three years, Marco was in a relationship with a man he describes as "magnetic — the kind of person who filled every room." In the beginning, the relationship felt like something he had waited his whole life for. The first incident happened about eight months in — a shove during an argument that left Marco against a kitchen wall, stunned more by disbelief than pain. His partner apologized for hours afterward. Marco told himself it was an aberration. It wasn't. Over the following two years, the physical violence escalated in frequency and severity: punches, objects thrown, one occasion in which he was choked until he lost consciousness briefly. He stayed, in part because of shame — he works with survivors every day and could not reconcile what was happening to him with the person he believed himself to be. He also stayed because leaving felt, for a long time, more frightening than remaining.

He eventually left after a particularly violent episode left him with a fractured rib. The divorce was finalized fourteen months ago. He has not spoken to his former partner since.

Marco presents now as a man who looks composed but feels fractured underneath. He sleeps poorly, waking most nights between two and four in the morning with his heart already racing, sometimes unsure for a moment where he is or whether he is safe. He has recurring nightmares — not always exact replays of what happened, but close enough: confined spaces, hands, the inability to make a sound. During the day, he moves through his work with professionalism, but certain things undo him without warning. A client raising their voice in frustration. The sound of something shattering in the break room. A colleague standing too close behind him. In those moments, his body responds before his mind can catch up — his chest tightens, his vision narrows, and he has to excuse himself to the bathroom to breathe through what he won't name to anyone as a panic attack.

He has become hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him. He sits facing the door in restaurants. He checks the locks in his apartment two or three times before bed. He has declined every social invitation from friends over the past six months, finding reasons that sound plausible — work, fatigue, prior commitments. The truth is that being around couples, or men who remind him in any way of his former partner, produces a dread he cannot explain and does not want to have to explain.

What troubles Marco most, and what he speaks about with a particular kind of grief, is the erosion of something he once took for granted: his capacity to feel safe in his own body. He describes feeling detached from himself during stressful moments, watching from a slight distance as if he is not quite inhabiting his own life. He has also begun to question his professional judgment in ways he never did before — wondering whether his empathy for clients is real or performed, whether he truly understands suffering or simply catalogues it.

He came to therapy, he says, because a client he had been supporting through a domestic violence situation looked at him one afternoon and asked if he was okay. He had no answer. He sat with that silence for two weeks before making the call. He is here now, and he is trying.
